newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Sanctions on Iraq to continue under Saddam, US official.
newsitem.headline: Sanctions on Iraq to continue under Saddam, US official.

text.p: The United States sees no practical alternative to maintaining sanctions against Iraq as long a President Saddam Hussein remains in power, a U.S. official said on Monday.

Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau said U.S. policymakers believe the Iraqi army would soon be back on the borders of Kuwait should the sanctions be removed or the United States reduce its own military posture in the Gulf.

"With the current Iraqi government ruthlessly and resiliently maintaining power in Baghdad....and with mistrust and lack of cohesion among various elements of the opposition, the United States sees no practical alternative to maintaining the box around Baghdad as tightly as possible," Pelletreau said in a keynote address at an international forum on Middle East Petroleum which started in Cyprus.
The three-day conference, organised by the International Business Communications group, will examine legal and political effects of sanctions on Iraq, Iran and Libya.

Iraq has not given up its ambitions to be a dominant power in the oil-rich Gulf region and the U.N. oil-for-food deal with Baghdad does not signal the beginning of the end of sanctions, Pelletreau told delegates.

He said the agreement, which allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over a six month period and import food and medical supplies to its suffering people, has made the international coalition stronger.
"It has removed the argument that some were making that the United Nations was somehow responsible for the suffering of the Iraqi people, not their own government," Pelletreau added.
Iraq has been under U.N. sanctions since its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The trade curbs place a blanket ban on its oil exports and investments in the country.
Pelletreau, former Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs between February 1994 and January 1997, said Iraq was now on its "best behaviour".
"My guess is that unless there are serious new Iraqi transgressions in the meantime, the oil-for-food programme is likely to be renewed at the same level for another six months."

Pelletreau disclosed that the United States protested to Moscow over a post-sanctions agreement signed between Iraq and Russia on March 21 to develop seven to eight billion barrels of reserves in Iraq's southern Qurna oilfield.
Moscow has said it would not violate the international trade curbs on Baghdad.
He said Washington sought and obtained Russian assurances the sanctions would be scrupulously respected.
Pelletreau expressed support for an authorised dialogue between Washington and Iran "in which its objections to Iranian policy could be raised", he said.
Iran has been under a U.S. trade and investment ban since 1995 on charges of sponsoring terrorism and seeking to develop nuclear weapons. Iran denies the charges.

"A number of voices in the United States, including my own, have begun to recommend opening this door to dialogue even wider," he said. "There is no reason that the United States should shrink from a full-agenda dialogue with Iran. It should welcome it."

But Pelletreau said that if inquiries reveal Iranian involvement in the al-Khobar bombing in Saudi Arabia which killed 19 U.S. servicemen last year, the United States will possibly demand the imposition of U.N. sanctions on Tehran.
"Such a development would set back the prospects for eventual reconciliation considerably," he said.
